summaries.example: Imagine joining a club because you enjoy playing games with its members. Stirner might say this is different from believing you must obey the club forever, even when you no longer want to. He calls a flexible friendship or group like this a “union of egoists”: people cooperate for their own reasons while each keeps making their own choices.
summaries.summary: Max Stirner was a nineteenth-century German thinker best known for The Ego and Its Own. He argued that people often obey forces that they treat as higher than themselves. These forces can include religion, the state, society, moral rules, or an idea of what a “proper human being” should be. Stirner called for “ownness,” meaning that each person should remain their own master. His egoist is not simply a greedy person. Instead, an egoist tries not to become a tool of outside rules or even of one narrow desire. Stirner rejected fixed duties, including a general duty to obey the state or always keep promises. He proposed a “union of egoists,” where independent people join together when cooperation serves their purposes. The Stanford Encyclopedia notes that his writing is difficult and provocative, and that scholars disagree about whether some of his claims are arguments, jokes, or deliberate challenges. His work damaged confidence in the left-Hegelian movement, influenced Karl Marx’s thinking, and later became important to individualist anarchism.
key_ideas: Stirner argued that people can be controlled not only by rulers and laws but also by ideas that seem sacred or unquestionably true.
He criticized thinkers who replaced belief in God with belief in a fixed idea of “human nature.”
He valued being one’s own master more highly than following permanent moral duties.
He imagined people cooperating in changing groups while keeping their independence.
His book was written in a surprising, playful, and sometimes shocking style, so readers have disagreed about how seriously to take every claim.
summaries.why_it_matters: Stirner’s ideas make us ask who or what guides our choices. They also raise a difficult question: how can people live together if nobody has a permanent duty to obey shared rules? His work is useful for thinking about freedom, friendship, laws, promises, and the difference between choosing for yourself and simply chasing whatever you want.

important_terms.definition: A person’s ability to direct their own life and choices instead of being controlled by someone or something else.
Stirner’s name for being one’s own master. It means not letting other people, rules, ideas, or even strong feelings completely control you.
Stirner’s word for a person who tries to remain self-ruling. It does not simply mean someone who wants money or always acts selfishly.
A temporary group in which people cooperate because it helps them, without giving up their independence.

questions_to_think_about: Can working with other people help us stay independent?
Are rules always controlling, or can some rules be useful?
Can a person be caring and still make their own choices?
Why might a writer use jokes or shocking examples when discussing serious ideas?

summaries.example: Consider a student who joins a campaign group to support a cause. A conventional view might say that joining creates duties to the group or that the cause expresses a shared moral ideal. Stirner would ask whether the student remains self-directing or has made the group, its rules, or its ideal into a power over them. His “union of egoists” allows cooperation, but only as a changing association whose value comes from what its members gain; it has no shared final purpose that permanently commands them.
summaries.summary: Max Stirner’s The Ego and Its Own is a polemical critique of modern philosophical and political thought. Its central target is subordination: the condition in which an individual treats an external or internal power as entitled to command them. Stirner claims that modern thinkers who reject Christianity may preserve its structure by elevating abstractions such as humanity, reason, conscience, citizenship, labor, or critical activity above actual individuals. His alternative is egoism, more precisely “ownness,” in which the individual is self-ruling. The entry emphasizes that this position should not be reduced to psychological egoism, the claim that every action is motivated by self-interest, or to conventional material selfishness. Stirner condemns the wealthy miser who becomes enslaved to money, because being ruled by one’s own single aim is still a loss of autonomy. His view also is not straightforward nihilism: although he rejects morality as a system of fixed obligations, he positively evaluates autonomy and the character of the self-ruling individual. This leads him to deny inherent political obligation and any general duty to keep promises. He sketches a union of egoists as a flexible, instrumental association among independent people. The source notes, however, that this proposal leaves unresolved whether relationships such as love, trust, and care can retain their familiar meaning when they are valuable only insofar as they serve the individual. Stirner’s style—hyperbolic, playful, and structurally related to Hegelian development—makes interpretation difficult. His historical importance includes his disruptive effect on left-Hegelianism, his influence on Marx’s intellectual development, and his later role in individualist anarchism.
key_ideas: Stirner’s tripartite structure presents childhood realism, youthful idealism, and adult egoism as an analogy for ancient, modern, and future historical stages.
He argues that modernity did not fully escape religion because it can place “spirit,” conscience, reason, or an idealized humanity above the individual.
His criticism of Feuerbach targets the replacement of God with a supposedly universal human essence; Stirner claims this merely changes the master.
Egoism is best understood in the entry as a demanding form of individual self-rule, including detachment from one’s own appetites and projects, not as ordinary pursuit of wealth.
Stirner rejects morality understood as fixed obligations, including political obligation and a general duty to keep promises, because such duties can subordinate the individual.
The proposed union of egoists offers cooperation without permanent allegiance, but its instrumental character creates serious questions about trust, care, and social stability.
summaries.why_it_matters: Stirner presses a conflict at the heart of political philosophy: individual freedom may be threatened by rulers, but cooperation seems to require expectations, promises, and shared standards. His work therefore tests whether autonomy can coexist with obligation. It also challenges theories that appeal to a universal human essence, asking whether such ideals describe people or impose a new authority. Even when one rejects his conclusions, his distinction between self-rule and merely pursuing one’s strongest desire remains philosophically useful.

important_terms.definition: Stirner’s term for self-mastery: the individual remains able to judge and act rather than being subordinated to external authorities or internal impulses.
Stirner’s preferred ideal of a person who refuses subordination and treats individual self-rule as the highest value. This is not identical to ordinary greed or self-interest.
The view that all intentional actions are motivated by the agent’s self-interest. The entry notes that Stirner should not simply be classified as defending this view.
An association of independent people who cooperate temporarily for their advantage without creating a shared authority or final common purpose.
A theory that human beings have a fixed or universal nature that can tell us how we ought to live. Stirner attacks this kind of perfectionism.
A system or institution that claims authority over people. Stirner argues that the state necessarily conflicts with self-rule because law presents obligations to obey.
The view that there are no values or standards at all. The entry distinguishes this from Stirner’s rejection of morality, since he still ranks autonomy above other goods.

questions_to_think_about: If a person chooses to follow a rule, can that rule still count as a form of subordination?
Does Stirner’s account successfully distinguish autonomy from impulsive or narrow self-interest?
Can promises, love, or political cooperation survive if no obligation is binding in itself?
Is rejecting fixed moral duties the same as rejecting all values?
Should Stirner’s extreme examples be read as conclusions of his theory, provocations, or both?

summaries.example: Suppose a group of friends creates a study team. At first, everyone joins because working together helps them. Later, the group starts saying that a “real member” must attend every meeting and never disagree. Stirner would ask whether the team has become a power over its members. He would prefer a flexible association: people can cooperate when it benefits them, leave when it does not, and avoid treating the group as permanently entitled to command them.
summaries.summary: Max Stirner was a nineteenth-century German writer whose major book, The Ego and Its Own, attacks the ways people become subject to powers they have created or accepted. He includes ordinary authorities such as the state, but also less visible powers: religion, conscience, reason, morality, and ideal pictures of human nature. Stirner argues that some modern thinkers thought they had defeated religion by rejecting God, yet still placed “humanity” or another spiritual ideal above actual individuals. He calls for egoism, which the entry explains most clearly as ownness: the ability to remain one’s own master. This is not the same as greed or the claim that every action is psychologically selfish. A person can lose self-rule by becoming devoted to money, a cause, a feeling, or a social role. Stirner therefore values a kind of independence from both outside commands and inner forces that take control. He rejects morality when it means fixed duties that bind everyone, and he denies that laws or promises automatically create obligations. His view of the state is especially radical because he sees obedience to law as incompatible with complete autonomy. Still, he does not picture the future as total isolation. He proposes unions of egoists: temporary, useful cooperation among people who remain independent. The source also points out a tension in this proposal. Stirner sometimes suggests that love and other familiar relationships can continue, but his account allows them only while they contribute to the individual’s own experience and self-rule. His book’s unusual style, wordplay, exaggeration, and three-part historical structure make interpretation challenging. key_ideas: Stirner says modern people may still think religiously when they obey ideas such as “humanity,” “reason,” or “morality” as if these ideas were higher powers.
He argues that replacing God with an ideal human nature does not necessarily free people; it may create a new standard that judges and controls everyone.
His egoism means self-rule, not simply selfishness, wealth-seeking, or doing whatever one feels like doing.
He rejects fixed moral duties and argues that even laws and promises cannot automatically bind a self-ruling person.
He imagines a union of egoists as cooperation without permanent membership, loyalty, or a shared final goal.
The entry presents Stirner as difficult to classify and notes his later influence on individualist anarchism and his importance in Marx’s intellectual development.
summaries.why_it_matters: Stirner’s philosophy helps readers examine the hidden authorities behind everyday choices. It asks whether freedom means merely choosing, or whether it requires resisting ideas, groups, and desires that take command of us. His argument also exposes a practical problem: people need cooperation, but cooperation can create pressure to obey. Thinking through that problem can clarify disagreements about laws, friendship, political membership, and personal independence.

important_terms.definition: Being able to guide your own choices instead of being ruled by another person, an institution, or an idea.
Stirner’s term for self-mastery. A person has ownness when they do not let outside authorities or their own uncontrolled desires make them into instruments.
A person who seeks self-rule. Stirner’s egoist is not simply greedy and is not automatically someone who always seeks money or comfort.
A changeable partnership in which people cooperate for their own purposes without surrendering their independence.
A belief that people share a fixed human nature that can determine what everyone ought to do. Stirner criticizes this kind of theory.
The organized political authority that makes and enforces laws. Stirner sees its demand for obedience as opposed to complete self-rule.

questions_to_think_about: When does a helpful group become controlling?
Can an ideal such as justice guide us without becoming a power over us?
How is self-rule different from following every impulse?
Would trust be possible if promises were never binding?
Why might scholars disagree about whether Stirner was a nihilist?
